blocks.text: **The problem.** Given the `root` of a binary tree, return its **left view**: the values you would see standing to the **left** of the tree — the **first** (leftmost) node of every level, from top to bottom.

blocks.alt: Looking at the tree 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, null, 8 from the left: on each level only the leftmost node is visible. The left view is 1, 2, 4, 8. Node 8 is visible even though it is a right child, because nothing else is on its level.

elements.text: 8 is a right child, but the
elements.originalText: 8 is a right child, but the

blocks.code:
Input:  root = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, null, 8]     Output: [1, 2, 4, 8]
Input:  root = [1, null, 2, null, 3]              Output: [1, 2, 3]
Input:  root = []                                 Output: []

blocks.text: It's tempting to just follow left children down from the root — but that's wrong: on a level where the left side has run out, the leftmost node may be a **right** child, deep in the right subtree. The second example has no left children at all. What we need is **the first node of each level**.
1. Brute force: list every level, keep the first
Do a full level order traversal, storing every level, then take the first value of each.
**Time O(n), space O(n)** — it stores every value of the tree just to keep one per level.
2. Optimal: breadth-first, keep the front of each level
No need to store levels: at the start of each round, the **front of the queue** is the leftmost node of that level. Record it, then process the round as usual.
**Time O(n), space O(w)** for the queue — up to about n / 2 for a full tree.
3. Best solution: depth-first, first to reach each depth

A preorder walk that always goes **left before right** reaches every depth for the first time through that depth's **leftmost** node. So pass the depth down, and record a node exactly when `depth === view.length` — the first time anyone has reached this depth. No queue at all.

blocks.alt: Preorder visits 1, 2, 4, 8, 5, 3, 6, 7. The first node to reach depth 0 is 1, depth 1 is 2, depth 2 is 4, depth 3 is 8. Every later node arrives at a depth that already has a value and is skipped.

blocks.caption: Watch which node is the first to reach each depth — even when it's a right child.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(h)** — the call stack holds one root-to-node path, which for a balanced tree is far smaller than its widest level.

rows.timeWhy: Each node is **queued and dequeued once**.
rows.spaceWhy: The queue holds a level: up to about **n / 2** for a full tree.

rows.timeWhy: Each node is visited **once**, left child first.
rows.spaceWhy: The call stack holds **one path**: far less than the widest level.

items: **A deep level reached only from the right** — the example's 8.
**A perfect tree** — exactly the leftmost spine.
**Right Side View** (LeetCode 199) — visit the **right** child first in the DFS, or keep the **last** node of each BFS level.
**Top View / Bottom View** — viewing by column instead of by level (next lesson).
**Boundary Traversal** — the left boundary, then the leaves, then the right boundary in reverse.
